title: Burn it or bury it: Montgomery County at a waste management crossroads, with no easy answers
summary: Calls to retire Montgomery County's trash incinerator at Dickerson present complex environmental, health and equity tradeoffs, write Vivian Thomson and Kit Gage, and county residents will need more facts than they have to make the right decision.
content:
by Vivian E. Thomson and Kit Gage, Maryland Matters November 19, 2025

by Vivian E. Thomson and Kit Gage, Maryland Matters November 19, 2025

Montgomery County is at a waste management crossroads. The county has issued a request for proposals to export its 600,000 tons of annually generated waste to a landfill, probably in another state. County Executive Marc Elrich has long pushed to close the county’s trash incinerator.

This decision involves complicated environmental, public health, equity and cost tradeoffs, and the county lacks vital pieces of information. We have summarized what we know and what we don’t know in a report posted by Friends of Sligo Creek.

On the environmental and public health side of the equation, incinerators kill pathogens, but they produce carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. Still, our analysis indicates that landfilling the county’s waste could produce far more greenhouse gases than incinerating it. That’s because landfills emit methane, an especially potent greenhouse gas.

The incinerator’s air pollution controls appear to be working well. The county’s solid waste plan says, “Several health-risk assessment studies have concluded that there are no measurable influences on ambient air concentrations attributable to RRF [incinerator] source emissions” (p. 3-32). According to the Maryland Department of the Environment, the incinerator operates well within its permitted air pollution limits and, except for hydrogen chloride, within the Biden administration’s proposed stricter standards for waste incinerators.

But the incinerator’s ash, a source of toxic metals, currently goes to a Richmond, Virginia, landfill whose surrounding community is 70% African American. County staff say the ash is stabilized to remain non-hazardous and that it is tested regularly.

Nearby jurisdictions use a different ash disposal technique. Arlington County, Fairfax County and the City of Alexandria use an ash monofill, a type of facility that’s designed to prevent the release of metals.

In extending the life of their incinerator to 50 years, Arlington and Alexandria said, “it was found to be economically beneficial for both jurisdictions.” They also cited the “stellar” environmental record of the facility. Although incinerators can divert materials from recycling, Arlington and Alexandria report strong recycling rates (53%), as does Montgomery County (45%).

Landfills harbor pathogens. They produce copious amounts of air and water pollution, for decades. Landfill gases contain carcinogens like benzene and vinyl chloride. Landfill leachate (garbage “juice”) is a toxic chemical cocktail, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has said that even the best-protected landfills will eventually leak. One Virginia megalandfill identified as a potential recipient of the county’s trash generates almost 400,000 gallons of leachate per week. That landfill is in bankruptcy proceedings.

Equity is an important consideration. The area near the county’s incinerator is relatively well-off and is disproportionately white (75% white alone, versus 40% for the whole county). Many Virginia landfills are in marginalized communities. Maryland is already the leading out-of-state contributor to Virginia’s trash imports. The principles of proximity and self-sufficiency encourage the treatment of waste close to its point of origin.

Dueling estimates cloud the cost picture.

The county’s 2025 contractor report projects that, in the long term, even with needed upgrades, using the incinerator would be cheaper than landfilling. In 2024, the facility generated $24 million in revenues from sales of electricity and recovered metals. Closing the incinerator would mean losing those revenues and burying metals that, when recycled, save energy and reduce greenhouse gas pollution relative to using virgin materials.

However, county staff maintain that, in the short term, the landfill-plus-incinerator-closure option would be cheaper than continuing to operate the incinerator. They argue that the incinerator’s expenses would divert resources from efforts to decrease the county’s waste stream and that paying for landfilling on a per ton basis would incentivize waste reduction. However, the county has not estimated closure costs for the incinerator.

Some important unknowns are: The likely substantial costs for closing the county’s incinerator and remediating its site; the cost to send the incinerator’s ash to a different disposal site; and, the cost to extend the life of the incinerator, because no request for proposals has been issued to that end. For the landfill option, we don’t know what the impacts on the Derwood transfer station might be or whether the county might be liable for landfill contamination problems.

Finally, we don’t know what the county’s citizens think. The county has not scheduled a public hearing.

Council members say we must keep all options open and express deep unease with — or outright opposition to — exporting our trash. They, and the county’s citizens, deserve to see the full picture, and members of the public should have an opportunity to comment.
